days.title: Secrets in Terraform: State and Plan Exposure, Ephemeral Values, Write-Only Arguments and Rotation

concepts.heading: sensitive Hides Display, Not Storage
concepts.body: Marking a variable or output `sensitive = true` changes how Terraform displays a value: it is redacted in CLI output and in the HCP Terraform UI, and any expression that references it is treated as sensitive too. It does not change what Terraform stores. State and plan files still contain the real value, so anyone who can read them can read the secret, and `terraform output -raw` or `-json` prints a sensitive output in plain text. A typical failing review: a module passes `var.db_password` (sensitive) to `aws_db_instance`, the plan shows `(sensitive value)`, yet an auditor opens the state file and sees the password. The fix is not another flag on the variable but keeping the value out of state altogether, plus protecting the state backend as the secret store it effectively is. The same holds for saved plans: `terraform plan -out` writes the full configuration, all values for planned changes and the input variables, and the documentation says sensitive data is saved in cleartext in the plan file. A pipeline that uploads `tfplan` as a build artifact must therefore restrict who can download it and keep retention short, exactly as for state.

concepts.heading: Ephemeral Resources and Write-Only Arguments
concepts.body: Only ephemeral values are omitted from state and plan files: variables and child module outputs with `ephemeral = true`, `ephemeral` blocks and write-only arguments. An ephemeral resource such as `ephemeral "random_password" "db" {}` exists only during the current operation and is never written to state or plan. A write-only argument, usually named with a `_wo` suffix such as `password_wo`, is a managed-resource argument that the provider uses when it creates or updates the object and that Terraform then discards. It needs Terraform 1.11 or later and provider support. To get a generated password into a database without a trace in state, feed the ephemeral value into the write-only argument: `password_wo = ephemeral.random_password.db.result`. Replacing `password = random_password.db.result` with a sensitive variable would still store it. Write-only arguments accept ephemeral and non-ephemeral values, but a literal string would still sit in the configuration, so HashiCorp recommends feeding them from an ephemeral resource. Because the value is not stored, the plan cannot show a diff for it, which matters for rotation.

concepts.heading: Where an Ephemeral Value May Be Used
concepts.body: Terraform allows references to ephemeral values only where the value cannot be persisted: `locals`, `variable` blocks with `ephemeral`, child module `output` blocks with `ephemeral`, write-only arguments of managed resources, other `ephemeral` blocks, `provider` blocks, and provisioner and connection blocks. Anywhere else, for example an ordinary resource argument, a data source or a root output, planning returns an error. That list answers the question of a team that reads a secret with `ephemeral "aws_ssm_parameter" "api"` and wants to use `.value`: a write-only argument and a provider configuration are valid, an ordinary argument or a root output is not. Ephemeral outputs are the way a module hands a short-lived credential to its caller during one run, but the `ephemeral` argument on an output is allowed only in child modules, since a root output is persisted so that `terraform output` and other configurations can read it. If a root module re-exports `module.auth.token` as an ephemeral output, `terraform validate` fails; the root should consume the value in an ephemeral context such as a provider block instead. Note that `sensitive` on a child output is a different control: it hides the value on screen but the value still reaches state.

concepts.heading: Rotation: Version Arguments and Vault Leases
concepts.body: A rotation can be invisible. Terraform sends a write-only argument to the provider on every operation, but it keeps no prior value, so a new value alone produces no plan diff. A team sets `password_wo = var.new_password` and `password_wo_version = 1`, the pipeline supplies the rotated secret, and the plan says no changes while the database keeps the old password. The provider's version argument is the stored signal: Terraform does store that number, so incrementing it in the same change as the new value produces an update and the provider applies the new write-only value. Good practice ties the version to the secrets manager's own version metadata so that rotation in the store drives the update. Dynamic secrets have a lifecycle too. An `ephemeral` block opens when Terraform needs it (for a Vault secret the provider obtains a lease), renews if the operation outlasts the expiration, and closes after dependent providers finish in that phase, which for Vault explicitly ends the lease so the credentials are revoked immediately. If an input to an ephemeral resource is unknown until apply, such as the ID of a secret version created in the same run, Terraform defers the ephemeral resource to the apply stage; a data source for the same read would have stored the value in state.

concepts.heading: Leak Paths Outside State: VCS, Variables and Credentials
concepts.body: Variable files are plain text and Git keeps history. A reviewer who finds `prod.auto.tfvars` with `db_password` committed two weeks ago must treat the secret as compromised: deleting the file does not remove it from earlier commits, clones or forks. The complete fix has three parts: rotate the credential, remove and ignore the file (rewriting history is an extra clean-up, never a substitute for rotation) and re-supply the value from outside the repository, such as an HCP Terraform sensitive variable, an environment variable or an ephemeral read from a secrets manager. A related review point concerns provider credentials stored in a workspace. A sensitive Terraform variable is unreadable in the UI and API, but Terraform runs receive the full text of all variable values and may print them in logs or state if the configuration sends them to an output or a resource argument. A provider credential supplied as an environment variable is read by the provider process and is not referenced from the configuration, so that path does not exist; both categories can be marked sensitive. Better still is to remove the stored secret: dynamic credentials, either through the platform's workload identity or through Vault, issue short-lived values per run (covered on the next day).

examPoints: A question where a sensitive variable still appears in the state file is testing that sensitive only redacts display; the answer that keeps it out of state uses an ephemeral value with a write-only argument.
A question about a rotation that produces an empty plan is testing the write-only version argument: increment it together with the new secret so that the stored number changes.

A question about an ephemeral value used in an ordinary resource argument, a data source or a root output is testing the list of allowed ephemeral contexts; locals, write-only arguments, provider blocks and child module ephemeral outputs are valid.

quiz.q: A config passes `random_password.db.result` to the `password` argument of `aws_db_instance`. Security wants the generated password in neither resource's state entry. Which change achieves this?
choices: Mark the `random_password` result as sensitive in an output and keep `password` as the argument
Store the password in a variable with `sensitive = true` and pass `var.password` to `password`
Make the generator an `ephemeral "random_password"` block and pass its result to a write-only argument such as `password_wo`
Keep the resources and add the `-out` plan file to a private artifact store
quiz.explain: The ephemeral block is never written to state or plan, and the write-only argument is discarded after the provider uses it, so neither entry holds the password. Choices A and B only hide the display and the value stays in state; choice D protects a plan file but does nothing for state.

quiz.q: A database sets `password_wo = var.new_password` and `password_wo_version = 1`. The secret was rotated and the pipeline passes the new value, but `terraform plan` shows no changes. What is the correct explanation and fix?
choices: Terraform keeps no prior value of a write-only argument, so there is nothing to compare; increment the version argument with the new value
Write-only arguments are refreshed only by `terraform apply -refresh-only`, so run that first
The variable must be marked `sensitive = true` for Terraform to detect the new value
State locking hides the diff; force-unlock the workspace and plan again
quiz.explain: The write-only value is never stored, so only the stored version number can signal a change. Choice B is wrong because refresh does not read an argument that was never saved, and choices C and D concern display and locking, not change detection.

days.recap: Sensitive hides display only; state and saved plans hold cleartext. Ephemeral resources, variables and child outputs plus write-only arguments keep secrets out of state, usable only in allowed contexts. Rotate with the *_wo_version argument, let Vault leases close with the run, and never leave secrets in VCS.

days.title: Pipeline Identity, Policy Sets and Risky Changes: Least Privilege, Sentinel/OPA Scope and Plan Gates

concepts.heading: Workload Identity and Trust Policies
concepts.body: With dynamic provider credentials, HCP Terraform generates a workload identity token (a JWT) for each plan or apply, signed with its private key and expiring at the end of the run phase. The cloud verifies it with the platform's public key and returns temporary credentials for the role named in the workspace variables, so nothing long-lived is stored. That is the direct answer to a team that rotates an IAM user key by hand in a sensitive environment variable. The trust policy is where least privilege is decided. The `sub` claim reads `organization:ORG:project:PROJECT:workspace:WS:run_phase:PHASE`, and HashiCorp's guidance is to match at least `aud` (the intended audience, so a token issued for one system cannot be replayed against another) and `sub`. A `StringLike` pattern with `*` for project and workspace lets every workspace in the organization, including a sandbox any developer can run, assume a production admin role; if the organization name is not matched at all, any workspace on HCP Terraform could reach the cloud resources. Use the exact project and workspace, and wildcard only the run phase when plan and apply need the same access. Claims such as `terraform_run_id` change on every run, so they are useless for trust matching.

concepts.heading: Separate Plan and Apply Roles, and Vault-Backed Credentials
concepts.body: The `sub` claim ends in `run_phase:plan` or `run_phase:apply`, so trust policies can tell the phases apart. For a workspace whose plans should only read and whose applies must write, create two roles, each trusting one phase, and set the environment variables `TFC_AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN` and `TFC_AWS_APPLY_ROLE_ARN`; if the plan variable is absent, `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` is used for both. A wildcard on `run_phase` or a longer session duration cannot create this separation. There are two forms of dynamic credentials. The first relies on the cloud trusting the platform's OIDC identity and verifying tokens through its public metadata endpoints. The second, Vault-backed dynamic credentials, authenticates the run's token to Vault, whose secrets engines (AWS, GCP, Azure) generate short-lived credentials. The documentation positions Vault-backed credentials for teams that want a central place to manage cloud credentials and want to avoid exposing the platform's OIDC metadata endpoints publicly. A self-hosted Terraform Enterprise instance with no public metadata endpoint that still needs short-lived AWS credentials therefore fits the Vault-backed form.

concepts.heading: Permissions Add Up and Connected Systems Count
concepts.body: HCP Terraform permissions are additive across organization, project and workspace scopes: a team's effective permission is the highest level it holds from any scope. If a team has the Read role on workspace prod-net but also holds the organization permission Manage all workspaces, its members can queue and confirm applies there. The reverse does not apply: a lower organization permission such as View all workspaces never overrides a higher workspace role. Least-privilege reviews must therefore audit all scopes together and grant only the workspace or project roles that are intended. Permissions of integrated systems count too. In a VCS-connected workspace, anyone who can merge to the linked branch can queue plans, even without permission to queue plans and even if they are not an organization member; with auto-apply on, merging also starts the apply. Developers with only Read on the workspace but merge rights on main therefore hold an effective write path. Treat merge rights as workspace write rights: protect the branch, require reviews, limit who can merge and turn auto-apply off on sensitive workspaces so a human or policy gate confirms the plan.

concepts.heading: Policy Sets: Scope, Enforcement and Who May Override
concepts.body: A policy set is a collection of policies, and scope lives on the set, not on the individual policy. It can be global, or limited to projects, workspaces or workspaces with specific tags, and it can exclude a project, workspace or tag. A tagging rule for every workspace except those in Sandbox, now and for workspaces created later, is a global policy set with Sandbox excluded; manual attachment has gaps whenever someone forgets. A baseline can run globally while stricter sets cover selected projects. Each policy has a framework, Sentinel or OPA, fixed at creation, and a set contains policies of one framework only. Sentinel levels are advisory (reported, never stops), soft mandatory (stops the run in the Policy Override state, and a user allowed to override can continue) and hard mandatory (stops until the configuration is fixed); if the set enables the override option, permitted users can override even hard failures. Team permissions decide who: no policy overrides, delegate policy overrides, or manage policy overrides. The Manage policies permission lets security staff write policies and set enforcement and implies reading runs on all workspaces, but not changing infrastructure. An OPA policy is registered with a query such as `data.terraform.policies.public_ingress.deny` whose result must be an array; an empty array passes, and the plan is available as `input.plan`.

concepts.heading: Spotting and Blocking Risky Changes
concepts.body: Three layers catch dangerous changes. First, read the plan as data: `terraform show -json tfplan` has a `resource_changes` array, each entry with `change.actions`. A replacement appears as `["delete","create"]` or, with `create_before_destroy`, `["create","delete"]`, so a gate must test that the list contains both actions; matching only `["delete"]` misses replacements. The optional `action_reason` explains why: `delete_because_no_resource_config` and `delete_because_no_module` mark deletions caused by removed configuration, for example a deleted `module "db"` call, while `replace_because_cannot_update` and `replace_because_tainted` mark routine replacements. Second, `prevent_destroy = true` makes Terraform reject any plan that destroys the object, including a forced replacement, so changing a non-updatable argument of a protected database errors and the safe path is a planned migration; it does not stop destruction when the resource block itself is removed, because lifecycle rules are not recorded in state. Third, a mandatory Sentinel or OPA policy over `resource_changes` also covers block removal. A `check` block, by contrast, only warns after the plan or apply and, with workspace health checks, is re-evaluated on a schedule; it never blocks.

examPoints: A question about long-lived keys in a workspace is testing dynamic provider credentials: a token per run, trusted by `aud` and `sub`, with separate plan and apply roles when permissions differ.

A question about a team whose Read role still allows applies is testing additive permissions across scopes, and merge rights on a VCS-driven workspace with auto-apply are an equivalent hidden write path.

A question about preventing or detecting destruction expects a layered answer: prevent_destroy for plans, a mandatory policy on resource_changes for block removal, and check blocks only as non-blocking warnings.

quiz.q: An AWS role trusts HCP Terraform with `StringLike` on `sub` of `organization:acme:project:*:workspace:*:run_phase:*` and grants admin access to production. What is the risk, and what narrows it?
choices: Every workspace in the organization, including a sandbox one, can assume the production role; match the exact project and workspace, wildcarding only the run phase
Only workspaces in the acme organization with apply permission can assume the role, so the pattern is safe as written
Tokens never expire under this pattern; shorten the session duration on the role
The `aud` claim already limits the role to one workspace, so no change is needed
quiz.explain: The wildcards let any acme workspace assume the role. Choice B is wrong because the cloud sees only the token claims, not HCP Terraform permissions, and D is wrong because `aud` identifies the audience and not the workspace.

quiz.q: A developer deletes a `module "db"` call from the root. A review gate must flag deletions caused by removed configuration but let routine replacements pass. Which gate design is correct?
choices: Block any plan whose actions contain only `["delete"]` and ignore all replacements
Require extra approval when actions contain delete and the reason is `delete_because_no_resource_config` or `delete_because_no_module`, letting `replace_because_cannot_update` pass
Rely on `prevent_destroy`, which also stops deletion when a module call is removed
Use a `check` block, which stops the run when a resource is deleted
quiz.explain: The two removal reasons identify deletions caused by removed configuration while replacement reasons are routine. Choice C is wrong because prevent_destroy is not recorded in state and does not protect removed blocks, and choice D is wrong because a failed check only warns.

days.recap: Replace stored keys with dynamic credentials and trust only the exact organization, project, workspace, aud and sub, with separate plan and apply roles. Permissions are additive and merge rights count. Policy sets scope by global, project, workspace or tag; gate risky changes on resource_changes actions and reasons.

days.title: Module Design: When to Extract, Composition, moved Blocks, Providers and the Output Contract

concepts.heading: When a Module Pays Off
concepts.body: A module is a set of resources managed together behind an interface of input variables and outputs. Its child resources become part of the caller's plan, apply and state, so a module is a unit of reuse and standardization and not a unit of isolation: a failed apply inside one module affects the whole run. Splitting a directory into `network.tf` and `database.tf` organizes code without any module. Sound reasons to extract are a pattern used repeatedly with small parameter differences, or a set of resources that encode decisions such as defaults, naming, composition of several resources and validation. A pass-through wrapper is the counter-example: a module `s3_bucket` with 25 variables passed one-to-one to a single `aws_s3_bucket`, no defaults and no extra logic, encodes nothing. Callers must learn both the module and the resource, and the author must update the wrapper whenever the provider adds, renames or deprecates an argument. It would be justified by default encryption, versioning, public access blocks and tags, or by creating the bucket, policy and lifecycle rules together. Ask what decision the module makes for the caller before extracting.

concepts.heading: Composition and Keeping the Tree Flat
concepts.body: Terraform's composition guidance favors dependency inversion: a module declares what it needs as inputs and the caller decides where those objects come from. An `app` module that must use a managed VPC in production and an existing shared VPC in development should take `vpc_id` and `subnet_ids` as inputs; the caller passes `data.aws_vpc.shared.id` in development and `module.network.subnet_ids` in production. The alternative, a module that creates its own network behind conditionals, grows complex and cannot coexist with a network owned elsewhere. The same design keeps working when the network later moves into its own configuration. The guidance also recommends a flat tree, about one level of child modules connected by expressions in the root. In a chain `platform` calls `network` calls `subnets` calls `routing`, a team that needs a custom routing policy finds that every level must forward a variable. Instead, the root calls `network` and `routing` as siblings and passes `module.network.subnet_ids` into `routing`; a caller with a special need can swap one building block for its own, and the wiring is visible in one place.

concepts.heading: Refactoring Safely with moved Blocks
concepts.body: Terraform tracks objects by address, and `aws_instance.web` and `module.web.aws_instance.web` are different addresses. Moving a resource into a new module without telling Terraform plans a destroy of the old address and a create of the new one. A `moved` block (`from = aws_instance.web`, `to = module.web.aws_instance.web`) lets Terraform rename the state entry before planning, so the plan shows no destroy. The same mechanism covers other refactors. Switching `count` to `for_each` needs one block per instance, such as `from = aws_subnet.private[0]` to `aws_subnet.private["a"]`; put inside a shared module, every caller that upgrades picks up the mapping on its next plan, and new callers ignore it. Adding `count = 3` to a module call with `moved { from = module.a  to = module.a[2] }` treats the existing objects as instance 2, so the plan creates only `module.a[0]` and `module.a[1]`. When a grown module is split into `x` and `y`, keep the old module as a backward-compatible shim that calls both and carries `moved` blocks; references in them resolve relative to the containing module, and a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and its children, not a sibling's.

concepts.heading: Providers and Modules
concepts.body: Provider configurations are global to a configuration and may be defined only in the root module. A reusable module must not contain `provider` blocks: a module with its own provider block cannot be called with `count`, `for_each` or `depends_on` and fails with an error such as `Module does not support count`, and removing the module would also remove the configuration its resources need for destruction. The module declares what it needs in `required_providers` (including aliases through `configuration_aliases`), and the caller passes configurations with `providers`. Configurations are inherited, requirements are not: a child module that creates `datadog_monitor` resources without its own `required_providers` entry for `DataDog/datadog` does not inherit the root's source address, and Terraform may look for a `hashicorp/datadog` provider instead. Provider association is static because Terraform decides it before expanding `count` and `for_each`. A single module call with `for_each` over three regions cannot select `aws.eu`, `aws.us` and `aws.ap` per instance; write one `module` block per configuration, for example `providers = { aws = aws.eu }` in each. Every instance of one module call receives the same provider configurations.

concepts.heading: The Output Contract and Versioning
concepts.body: Inputs and outputs are the module's public interface, and anything exposed can be depended on. An output of `value = aws_db_instance.this` puts the entire provider schema into the contract: a provider rename or a change of resource type breaks callers although the module's code did not change, and it carries attributes nobody asked for. Expose stable names with descriptions, such as `endpoint`, `arn` and `port`, and mark secrets `sensitive = true`. Registry modules use semantic versions and callers write constraints like `~> 2.0` on that basis. Renaming or removing an input or output is breaking and belongs in a major release; adding an optional input or a new output is a minor release. A maintainer who renames `vpc_id` to `network_id` in 2.3.0 breaks every `~> 2.0` caller; the graceful path adds `network_id`, keeps `vpc_id` (noting it as deprecated) and removes it in 3.0.0. Instance keys are part of the contract as well: changing a resource from `count` to `for_each` without `moved` blocks forces replacement. Ephemeral outputs may be declared only in child modules, never in the root, and their value must come from an ephemeral context.

examPoints: A question that offers a module with identical arguments to one resource is testing abstraction: extract when the module encodes defaults, composition or validation, not for pass-through wrappers.
A question about a refactor that plans a destroy and create is testing moved blocks for new addresses, including instance keys, with the mapping placed in the module so callers inherit it.
A question about a module failing with count or for_each is testing that provider blocks belong only in the root, and per-instance provider selection needs separate module blocks.

quiz.q: A team moves `aws_instance.web` from the root module into `module "web"` containing the same resource. The plan shows `aws_instance.web` to be destroyed and `module.web.aws_instance.web` to be created. Which change gives a plan with no destroy?
choices: Add `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` to the resource inside the module
Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` before planning
Set `prevent_destroy = true` on the resource in the root
Add `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = module.web.aws_instance.web }` to the configuration
quiz.explain: The moved block maps the old state address to the new one before planning. Choice A only reorders a replacement, choice B updates attributes and not addresses, and choice C would make the plan error instead of fixing it.

quiz.q: A shared module adds `provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }`, and a caller that sets `count = 2` on the module call now fails with `Module does not support count`. What is the correct fix?
choices: Remove the provider block from the module, declare the provider in its `required_providers`, and configure it in the root, passing it with `providers` if needed
Add `depends_on` to the module call so the provider initializes first
Replace `count` with `for_each` on the module call, which supports embedded provider blocks
Pin the module with `version = "~> 1.0"` so the provider block is ignored
quiz.explain: A module that contains its own provider blocks cannot use count, for_each or depends_on, so the configuration must come from the root. Choice C is wrong because for_each has the same limit, and choices B and D do not touch the cause.

days.recap: Extract modules for reuse and encoded decisions, never for pass-through wrappers; accept inputs rather than create what the caller owns and keep the tree flat. Use moved blocks for address changes, keep provider blocks in the root, and treat outputs and semantic versions as the contract.

days.title: Registry and terraform test: Version Selection, Publishing, Private Registry, Mocks and Run Blocks

concepts.heading: Module Sources and Version Selection
concepts.body: The `version` argument takes a constraint and works only for modules from a registry, the public Terraform Registry or an HCP Terraform private registry; local paths share the caller's repository and Git sources are not versioned this way. A call with `source = "git::https://git.example.com/net.git"` and `version = "1.2.0"` makes `terraform init` fail. For Git, select a revision with the `ref` query parameter (a tag, branch or commit SHA), as in `?ref=v1.2.0`; without `ref`, Terraform clones the default branch at HEAD, which changes over time. Module versions are not recorded in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, which covers provider selections and checksums only. Terraform uses the newest installed module version that meets the constraint; if an acceptable one is already installed, a plain `terraform init` keeps it, and with none installed (a fresh checkout or CI runner) it downloads the newest allowed. With `version = "~> 2.1"`, a laptop initialized when 2.4.0 was newest stays on 2.4.0 while CI selects 2.5.0 after it is published. `terraform init -upgrade` moves installed modules to the latest allowed version. Where reproducibility matters, pin an exact version.

concepts.heading: Publishing to the Public Registry
concepts.body: The public registry publishes modules directly from a public GitHub repository. Requirements: the repository is named `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>` (for example `terraform-aws-ec2-instance`, and NAME may contain hyphens), it has a short description, it follows the standard module structure with the root module's `.tf` files at the repository root, and it has release tags that are semantic versions, optionally prefixed with `v`. At least one such tag is needed to publish; tags that do not look like versions are ignored. A repository called `aws-vpc-module` with tags like `release-2024.03` therefore needs two changes: rename it to the required pattern and create semantic version tags such as `v1.0.0`. New versions appear when a correctly formed tag is pushed and the registry's webhook notifies it. The standard module structure is conventional: `main.tf`, `variables.tf` and `outputs.tf` plus `README.md` and `LICENSE` at the root; `modules/` holds nested modules, where one with a `README.md` is intended for external use and one without is internal; `examples/` holds example configurations. Calls to nested modules from the root should use relative paths such as `./modules/consul-cluster` so they stay part of the same package. This layout is advisory and Terraform does not enforce it.

concepts.heading: Private Registry Addressing and Monorepos
concepts.body: A registry source has the form `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`, and without a hostname Terraform uses the public registry. A private registry adds the hostname in front. For HCP Terraform the hostname is `app.terraform.io` and the namespace is the organization name, so module `vpc` for provider `aws` in organization `acme` is `app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws`, selected within 1.x from 1.4 with `version = "~> 1.4"`. Callers need credentials for the registry, for example from `terraform login`, but not access to the module's source repository. When one repository holds `modules/app` and `modules/db` and is published by tag, every valid semantic-version tag creates a version of both modules, so releasing app also releases db. The fix is the Module Tag Prefix: with prefix `app-`, the tag `app-v1.0.0` publishes version `v1.0.0` of app only, and db ignores it. The Source Directory setting tells the registry where each module's files are but does not decide which tags apply. HCP Terraform can also run a module's tests automatically, but only for modules published with the branch-based workflow (a branch and a version, no tag required); it then runs on every commit to the branch and is unavailable while the organization publishes from a single repository. Engineers can run the stored tests with `terraform test -cloud-run=`.

concepts.heading: Mocks and Overrides in terraform test
concepts.body: A mocked provider (`mock_provider "aws" {}`) returns the real provider's schema and fills computed attributes with fake data, by type: numbers are 0, booleans false and strings random 8-character alphanumeric values. By default that data is generated during apply, so in a `command = plan` run computed attributes remain known after apply and an assertion like `aws_s3_bucket.logs.arn != ""` cannot be evaluated. Setting `override_during = plan` on the mock makes Terraform generate data at plan time, and the attribute can also appear in `mock_resource`, `mock_data` and override blocks, which win over the provider-level setting. The mock does not know real formats. A module with a precondition on `startswith(aws_iam_role.r.arn, "arn:aws:iam::")` fails under the generic mock, so give the attribute a realistic value with `mock_resource "aws_iam_role" { defaults = { arn = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/test" } }`. Defaults can also live in `.tfmock.hcl` files. For modules, `override_resource` and `override_data` replace the computed values of a specific instance, and `override_module` with `outputs` replaces a whole module's outputs while Terraform creates none of that module's resources. This is how root-level assertions run without cloud credentials or S3 calls. Overrides can sit at file level or in a run block, where run level wins.

concepts.heading: Run Blocks: Failure Tests, Parallelism, Variables and Cleanup
concepts.body: `expect_failures` lists checkable objects (resources, data sources, `check` blocks, input variables, outputs) whose custom conditions are expected to fail; the run passes if they fail. Only the author's `validation`, `precondition`, `postcondition` and `check` conditions count, so a type mismatch still fails the run. By default run blocks execute one after another. With `parallel = true` on the `test` block or a run block, two runs execute together only if neither references the other's outputs, they use different state files, and both allow parallelism. The state file is chosen by `state_key` or, if unset, by module source, so independent runs against the main configuration share one state and gain no speed until each has its own `state_key`. At the end of a file Terraform destroys everything it created in reverse run block order, using the last run block that referenced each state: with setup (bucket module), init (main) and read (loader module) in that order, it destroys read's state, then main, then setup's, so the bucket is not deleted while objects remain. For variables, usual precedence applies except that values defined in the test file, file-level or run-level, are highest and override `-var`, variable files and environment variables, so `terraform test -var region=eu-west-1` loses to `variables { region = "us-east-1" }` in the file unless the run block sets its own value.

examPoints: A question that combines a Git source with a version argument is testing that version works only for registry modules; Git revisions use ref.
A question about a mocked test that cannot evaluate a computed attribute is testing override_during = plan, and a question about format-sensitive conditions is testing mock_resource defaults.
A question about parallel run blocks that gain nothing is testing separate state_key values and absent output references; about test variables, values in the test file win.

quiz.q: A module call has `version = "~> 2.1"`. A laptop was initialized when 2.4.0 was the newest release. 2.5.0 is now published and a CI job starts from a fresh checkout. With no extra flags, what do `terraform init` on the laptop and in CI select?
choices: Both select 2.5.0 because `.terraform.lock.hcl` records the newest module version
Both keep 2.4.0 because the constraint pins the installed minor version
The laptop selects 2.1.0 and CI selects 2.5.0 because init always picks the oldest matching version when no flag is given
The laptop keeps 2.4.0 and CI downloads 2.5.0, since module versions are not locked and an installed acceptable version is kept
quiz.explain: The lock file covers providers only, and plain init keeps an acceptable installed module while a fresh runner downloads the newest allowed. Choices A and B assume a lock that does not exist, and C describes behaviour Terraform does not have.

quiz.q: A test file sets `test { parallel = true }` and has four independent run blocks against the same module directory, with no `state_key` and no `module` blocks. It takes the same time as before. What is the reason and the fix?
choices: Run blocks never run in parallel when `command = plan` is used; switch to apply
They share the main configuration's state, so give each run block its own `state_key`
Parallelism needs `-parallelism=4` on the CLI; the test block setting is advisory
Parallel runs need `override_during = plan` on the mock provider
quiz.explain: Runs that share a state file execute sequentially, and state_key separates them. Choice A is wrong because plan runs can be parallel, choice C confuses the apply flag with the test setting, and choice D concerns mock data timing.

days.recap: The version argument is for registries only; Git uses ref and module versions are not locked. Public publishing needs terraform-PROVIDER-NAME, semantic tags and the standard layout; monorepos need tag prefixes. In terraform test, plan-time mocks, realistic defaults, overrides, state_key and test-file variables decide results.

days.title: Operating HCP Terraform: Execution Modes, Agents, Run Tasks, Workflows and VCS Triggers

concepts.heading: Execution Modes and Changing Them
concepts.body: A workspace has an execution mode that decides where Terraform runs. Remote: HCP Terraform runs plan and apply on its own disposable workers, and variables, variable sets, policies, cost estimation, notifications and VCS integration all work. Agent: the same lifecycle, executed by a `tfc-agent` in your network. Local: Terraform runs on your machine and the workspace only stores state. Project Default: the workspace inherits the mode from its project. Local mode has a consequence that shows up as a puzzling error: when credentials live in a variable set but the workspace is Local, an engineer's `terraform plan` fails with `no valid credential sources`, because HCP Terraform has nothing to inject into a process on the workstation. A plan belongs to the platform that made it, so changing the mode after planning breaks it: a team that switches a busy workspace from Remote to Agent finds that two runs which had finished planning fail on confirmation. Runs still queued have not planned and are unaffected. The safe sequence is to disable auto-apply, finish or discard any run that is no longer pending, lock the workspace, change the mode and pool, then re-enable auto-apply and unlock.

concepts.heading: Agents and Agent Hooks
concepts.body: An HCP Terraform agent (`tfc-agent`) runs inside a private network, belongs to an agent pool, and polls HCP Terraform for work. A workspace in Agent mode sends its plan and apply jobs to an available agent in the chosen pool. This is the answer for provisioning vSphere resources in a data center that accepts no inbound connections: the agent needs only outbound TCP connections, to the HCP Terraform APIs, the module registry, `releases.hashicorp.com` for Terraform binaries and the providers' own APIs (here the local vCenter). No inbound firewall rule is needed and runs keep variables, policies and notifications. Agent hooks are executables the agent runs at fixed points: `pre-plan`, `post-plan`, `pre-apply` and `post-apply`. The file name must be one of those four, so an agent has at most one hook per type. Each hook must be executable and has a timeout (60 seconds by default, at most 10 minutes). The pre-plan and pre-apply hooks run before `terraform init` in their operation. A non-zero exit code or a timeout fails the run. Environment variables do not carry from one hook to the next; to pass a variable to a later Terraform command, use the mechanism in the agent hooks documentation rather than a plain export.

concepts.heading: Run Tasks: Stages and Enforcement
concepts.body: Run tasks send a payload with a callback URL to an external service at pre-plan, post-plan, pre-apply or post-apply. The service must acknowledge with `200 OK` and then answer with `passed`, `running` or `failed`. The request errors if no progress update arrives within 10 minutes, and HCP Terraform treats a timeout or an unexpected remote error as failed. The enforcement level turns the result into an action: advisory shows a warning and the run continues, while mandatory stops the run (Plan Errored) on failure, including timeout or remote error. A mandatory post-plan scanner whose service is down therefore blocks every run that reaches that stage. When a run has several tasks, the most restrictive result applies. The stage decides the data: pre-plan runs before any plan exists, so its payload carries only the configuration version, while post-plan payloads include the JSON of the plan, which is what a scanner that analyzes planned changes needs. Run tasks call an external service you or a vendor operate; rules written and evaluated inside HCP Terraform are policy as code, covered on day 19.

concepts.heading: Three Workflows
concepts.body: A workspace is driven in one of three ways. VCS-driven: the workspace links to a branch of a repository, webhooks queue a run on each merge and pull requests get speculative plans, which cannot be applied; the code always comes from version control. CLI-driven: engineers run `terraform plan` or `apply` with a `cloud` block and the run executes in the workspace, so remote applies and saved plans work without a linked repository. API-driven: no repository is linked; your tooling decides when a run happens, packages the configuration as a `.tar.gz` with the configuration directory at the archive root, creates a configuration version through the API, uploads the archive and then creates the run. A pipeline that generates Terraform configuration from an internal service catalog and keeps no Git repository fits the API-driven workflow. With the CLI-driven workflow the Terraform version that executes a remote run is the workspace's version setting, not the engineer's local binary; the local binary is only the client.

concepts.heading: VCS Triggers: Paths, Tags and the First Run
concepts.body: When a VCS-backed workspace has a working directory, HCP Terraform uses it as the default filter and assumes only changes inside matter. In a monorepo with workspace working directory `envs/prod`, a change to a shared module under `modules/` starts no run. The Automatic Run Triggering options are: always trigger runs for any change (simple, but queues unneeded runs); trigger only when files in specified paths change, using patterns (globs, recommended) or prefixes (directories, including the working directory), and the same filter applies to speculative plans on pull requests; or trigger on git tags. The fix for the monorepo is to add a pattern or prefix covering `modules/`. Tag triggering needs the tag in one of these formats: semantic version (the whole tag, such as `0.4.2`), version with a prefix (`release-1.4.0`), with a suffix (`0.4.2-alpha`), or a custom regular expression. A production workspace that runs only when a release such as `release-1.4.0` is cut therefore uses the prefix format. One more rule: a new workspace with no runs does not accept runs from a VCS webhook, so several merged commits with an empty run list and no error under VCS events usually mean no one has started the initial run manually. A workspace also ignores a webhook for a commit SHA that it already created a run for.

examPoints: A question about runs failing with no credential sources on a laptop is testing Local execution mode, where workspace variables and variable sets are not injected.
A question about a closed data center is testing agents: outbound-only connections from the agent pool, and no inbound rule; mandatory run tasks fail the run on timeout.
A question about no run starting after a shared module change is testing working directory filtering, and an empty run list on a new workspace points to the manual initial run.

quiz.q: A company must provision vSphere resources in a data center that accepts no inbound connections from the internet and wants to keep HCP Terraform variables, policies and notifications. Which design fits?
choices: Switch the workspace to Local execution and run Terraform from a bastion host
Open an inbound firewall rule so HCP Terraform workers can reach vCenter
Use an API-driven workspace with remote execution and a VPN back to HCP Terraform
Run `tfc-agent` in the data center in an agent pool and set the workspace to Agent execution mode
quiz.explain: The agent polls outbound and keeps the full run lifecycle. Choice A loses variable injection and policies, choice B breaks the closed-network requirement, and choice C does not change where the run executes.

quiz.q: A mandatory post-plan run task calls an external scanner, and the scanner's service is down and never answers. What happens to runs that reach that stage?
choices: They continue with a warning because an unanswered task counts as passed
They wait indefinitely until the service responds
They stop in Plan Errored, because a timeout or unexpected remote error counts as failed and the task is mandatory
They skip the task and apply because only pre-plan tasks can block a run
quiz.explain: HCP Terraform treats a timeout as failed, and mandatory enforcement stops the run. Choice A would be right only for advisory, choice B ignores the 10 minute progress limit, and choice D is false because post-plan tasks can block.

days.recap: Execution mode decides where runs happen: Local gets no injected variables, and changing mode needs a lock and no finished plans. Agents need outbound access only; hooks and mandatory run tasks fail runs. Choose VCS, CLI or API workflows deliberately, and set trigger paths, tags and the first run.

days.title: HCP Terraform at Scale: Usage, Cost, Environments, Version Upgrades and Policy as Code in Pipelines

concepts.heading: Usage Counting and Cost Estimation
concepts.body: The Usage page counts managed resources by reading the state files of all workspaces and Stacks and counting entries whose mode is `managed`. Each resource instance is one: `count = 4` is four, and resources inside a module count, with a module called with `for_each` multiplying them. Data sources are not counted. A workspace with `aws_instance.web` using `count = 4`, a module with three `for_each` keys holding two queues each, one bucket and two data sources counts 4 + 3 x 2 + 1 = 11. The source is state, not configuration or execution mode, so scaling from `count = 2` to `20` adds eighteen. Cost estimation is off by default and is enabled by an organization setting. After each successful plan it shows hourly and monthly costs per resource, the monthly delta against current state and totals; it supports AWS, GCP and Azure resources and lists others as unestimated. It is an estimate, never a quota, and it is disabled for runs with `-target`. A Sentinel policy that blocks changes above a budget reads `tfrun.cost_estimate.delta_monthly_cost`. That read works with policy checks, but when the policy set is switched to the Agent type to use policy evaluations, the cost data is not available and the policy fails on every run.

concepts.heading: Multiple Environments: Projects, Variable Sets and Triggers
concepts.body: A project is a folder for workspaces in an organization, and it is the unit of delegation. Team permissions granted on a project apply to every workspace in it, including later ones, and variable sets can be scoped to a project so credentials apply automatically. For payments, search and data teams that each deploy dev, staging and prod and need their own admin rights and cloud credentials, use one project per team with team access and a project-scoped variable set, and dev, staging and prod as workspaces inside it. Moving a workspace between projects needs either the Manage all Projects organization permission or explicit team admin on both the source and destination projects, because the move changes who can read and write it. Same-key conflicts between variable sets resolve in a fixed order: priority sets first, then command-line values, workspace variables, variable sets from the most specific scope to the least (workspace, project, global), then `*.auto.tfvars` and `terraform.tfvars`. Within one scope and ownership, the lexical order of set names decides: `base-defaults` beats `team-overrides`, so `small` wins. Run triggers queue a run in a downstream workspace after a source run applies successfully; triggered runs do not auto-apply unless the separate Auto-apply run triggers setting is on. A project can also define an auto-destroy default after inactivity (state unchanged), with no approval prompt in the UI; use it for development.

concepts.heading: Upgrading Terraform Versions Across Workspaces
concepts.body: Two places hold a version: the workspace setting picks the binary HCP Terraform runs, and `required_version` in the `terraform` block says what the configuration supports; Terraform checks it at the start of each run. Merging `required_version = ">= 1.14.0"` into a workspace that is still on 1.12 makes every run fail at start. Upgrade the workspace first (or together with the change); removing the constraint only hides the incompatibility. To test a target version without touching the workspace, create a plan-only (speculative) run through the API with the plan-only option true and the `terraform-version` field set to the release. It runs with that version, is checked against policies, cannot be applied and ignores the run queue. With a `cloud` block and Remote execution, the workspace's version executes the plan even if the laptop runs 1.15. Agents are versioned separately: by default a `tfc-agent` updates itself to the latest minor version; `-auto-update` or `TFC_AGENT_AUTO_UPDATE` set `minor` (default), `patch` or `disabled`, and production pools commonly use `patch` or `disabled` plus planned upgrades. Some releases need a state format upgrade even when no resources change; Allow empty apply lets HCP Terraform apply a no-change plan so the state version is upgraded, and you should check the plan for drift first.

concepts.heading: Policy Enforcement in Runs
concepts.body: In a run, policies are evaluated after the plan (and cost estimation) and before apply. Sentinel failures: advisory only reports, soft mandatory stops the run in the Policy Override state until an authorized user overrides, hard mandatory stops it unless the set enables overrides. The strictest failure wins, so a run that fails one advisory, one soft and one hard policy in a set that cannot be overridden ends in Plan Errored, and auto-apply never starts. OPA policies are written in Rego, attached through policy sets, and run only as policy evaluations. They have two enforcement levels: advisory and mandatory, where a user with Manage Policy Overrides can override a mandatory failure; soft and hard belong to Sentinel. The policy query typically names `data.terraform.deny` and must return an array, which passes when empty. Because OPA runs as evaluations, it cannot read cost estimation data. Targeting changes what policies see: with `terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web`, the Sentinel `tfplan` imports see only the targeted subset, so a policy that insists `aws_s3_bucket.audit` appear in the plan fails although the bucket is configured correctly. Write policies that tolerate missing instances, or restrict targeted runs with a policy that checks `tfrun.target_addrs`.

concepts.heading: Publishing Policy and Choosing Between Policies and Run Tasks
concepts.body: Policies can reach HCP Terraform three ways: pasted into the UI (fine for experiments, not recommended for many policies), through a policy set connected to a repository so each push updates it, or through automation with the Policy Sets API or the `tfe` provider's `tfe_policy_set` resource. For a security team that tests policy code in CI and wants a new version to become active only after tests pass, the pipeline should push policy set versions by API or provider, so it controls when a version exists; policies are then applied through the set's scope (global, projects, workspaces or tags), not workspace by workspace. Note that a repository-connected set updates on each push, which would publish before the pipeline decides. Two extension points exist for gates in the run. Run tasks call an external service at pre-plan, post-plan, pre-apply or post-apply and return pass or fail, with advisory or mandatory enforcement. Policy as code puts the rules inside HCP Terraform as Sentinel or OPA. A security vendor's hosted service reviewing each plan with its own rules maps to a post-plan run task, since the plan JSON is in the payload; an in-house rule that production plans never open a security group to `0.0.0.0/0` maps to a policy in a policy set scoped to production.

examPoints: A question counting managed resources is testing state entries of mode managed: instances of count and for_each multiply, module instances multiply, data sources are excluded.

A question about a new required_version failing every run is testing the order: test with a speculative plan, upgrade the workspace, then merge the constraint; agent versions are controlled separately.

A question about gates in a pipeline expects the mapping: external vendor review is a run task, in-house rules are Sentinel or OPA policy sets, and CI publishes policy versions through the API or tfe provider.

quiz.q: A workspace state holds `aws_instance.web` created with `count = 4`, a module called with `for_each` over three keys containing two `aws_sqs_queue` resources, one `aws_s3_bucket` and two data sources. How many managed resources does HCP Terraform count?
choices: 8, because module instances are counted once
11, counting 4 + (3 x 2) + 1 and no data sources
13, because data sources are included
3, because it counts resource blocks, not instances
quiz.explain: Every managed instance in state counts and a for_each module multiplies its resources; data sources are excluded. Choice A ignores multiplication, choice C wrongly adds data sources, and choice D counts configuration blocks rather than state.

quiz.q: A pull request adds `required_version = ">= 1.14.0"` while the VCS-driven workspace is set to Terraform 1.12, and every run now fails at the start. What is the correct resolution?
choices: Delete the constraint from the configuration permanently
Upgrade the agent software with `TFC_AGENT_AUTO_UPDATE=minor`
Run Terraform 1.15 locally and push the state
Test with a speculative plan using the target version, set the workspace to that version, then merge the constraint
quiz.explain: The workspace setting picks the binary, so it must be upgraded before or with the constraint, after a plan-only run confirms compatibility. Choice A hides the incompatibility, and B changes the agent version, which is separate from the Terraform version.

days.recap: The Usage count is managed state entries, with instances and module instances multiplying and data sources excluded. Use projects for delegation and variable sets by scope. Upgrade a workspace before raising required_version, test with a speculative plan, and map vendor gates to run tasks and in-house rules to policy sets.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, the Seven Domains, Commonly Confused Pairs and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: The HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Infrastructure Engineer Professional (002) exam is multiple choice, online proctored and in English, lasts 90 minutes, and the credential is valid for 2 years. It tests Terraform 1.15 and the audience is an engineer who runs Terraform in production: shared modules, remote state, CI/CD, troubleshooting and governance. The number of questions, pass mark and domain weights are not published, so spread preparation evenly across the seven domains: 1 configuration, 2 state management and upgrades, 3 infrastructure workflow and lifecycle, 4 CI/CD and deployment, 5 security, secrets and compliance, 6 modules and the registry, 7 HCP Terraform operations. (The domain names are this guide's own labels.) Questions at this level are scenarios: a team reports a symptom, a plan shows something unexpected, or a requirement conflicts with a constraint, and you pick the diagnosis or the approach. Some items say how many answers to choose, so read the count and pick exactly that many. With 90 minutes, answer what you can decide quickly, flag long scenarios and return to them.

concepts.heading: Domains 1 to 3: Configuration, State and Workflow Pairs
concepts.body: Pairs that look alike are favorite wrong answers. `count` addresses instances by index, so removing a middle element shifts later instances and forces replacements, while `for_each` uses stable keys; a `moved` block maps old addresses to new ones for refactors from count to for_each or into modules. `sensitive` hides display only, while ephemeral values and write-only arguments stay out of state. `terraform apply -refresh-only` updates state to match reality without changing infrastructure, while `-replace` forces recreation of a chosen object. `-target` limits a run to chosen addresses for exceptions, and a saved plan from `plan -out` is applied exactly as reviewed. `create_before_destroy` changes the order of a replacement, `prevent_destroy` rejects plans that destroy but not removal of the whole block, and `ignore_changes` stops update proposals for named arguments. For upgrades, `required_version` constrains the CLI and the lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` records provider selections but not module versions. When a question describes a plan that will destroy something unexpectedly, trace the address: did a rename, a moved module or a changed key alter it?

concepts.heading: Domains 4 and 5: Pipelines, Identity and Secrets
concepts.body: A pipeline separates stages: format and validate early, produce a plan, review or approve, then apply the same saved plan. Speculative plans on pull requests show the result without the ability to apply. Dynamic provider credentials replace stored keys: HCP Terraform issues a workload identity token per run, and the cloud trust policy must match at least `aud` and `sub`, with exact project and workspace and, when plan and apply differ, separate roles by run phase. Vault-backed credentials fit when the platform cannot expose public OIDC metadata endpoints. Variable precedence still applies in pipelines, and sensitive values supplied as environment variables avoid leaking through outputs. Policy sets scope by global, project, workspace or tag and carry the enforcement level: Sentinel has advisory, soft mandatory and hard mandatory, OPA has advisory and mandatory. Permissions are additive across scopes, and merge rights on a VCS-driven workspace with auto-apply act as write access. Secrets in state, plan files and VCS history are all exposures: ephemeral resources plus write-only arguments keep them out of state, rotation of a write-only value needs the version argument, and a committed secret must be rotated.

concepts.heading: Domains 6 and 7: Modules, Registry and HCP Terraform
concepts.body: Modules are for reuse and encoded decisions, not isolation: they share the caller's state. Provider blocks belong only in the root module, requirements must be declared in each module's `required_providers`, and per-instance provider selection needs separate module blocks. Outputs and semantic versions form the contract; renaming an output is a major release. The `version` argument works only for registry modules and Git modules use `ref`. Public registry publishing needs `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>`, semantic tags and the standard layout; a monorepo in the private registry needs Module Tag Prefix. `terraform test` mocks fill computed values at apply by default, so plan-time assertions need `override_during = plan`; independent parallel runs need distinct `state_key` values. In HCP Terraform, Local mode gets no injected variables, agents need outbound access, and mandatory run tasks fail the run on timeout. The Usage page counts managed state entries. Projects delegate access and credentials, and upgrades go: speculative plan on the target version, workspace version, then `required_version`.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan
concepts.body: Read each scenario for the symptom first, then match it to one of the pairs above. For plan questions, ask whether a line comes from your code change or from drift, and whether an address changed. For security questions, ask where the value ends up: output, state, plan file, log or VCS. For governance questions, ask who can do what at which scope, and remember that scope sits on the policy set. For module questions, ask what the contract promises to callers. For HCP Terraform questions, ask where the run executes and which version, credentials and policies apply there. When two options both work, choose the one that is least privileged, reviewed before apply and consistent with the documented behavior, not the one that is merely possible. Eliminate options that rely on features outside Terraform 1.15 or on assumptions the question does not state. Do not change a correct answer without a concrete reason, and leave time to check the multiple-answer items against the count they ask for.

examPoints: Know that the exam is multiple choice, 90 minutes, Terraform 1.15, with the number of questions, pass mark and weights unpublished.
Expect scenario items: a symptom, a plan or a requirement, answered by diagnosis or by choosing between approaches, with distractors that are real features used in the wrong place.

Review the pairs that cause most mistakes: sensitive versus ephemeral, moved versus state commands, version for registries versus ref for Git, run tasks versus policy sets, workspace version versus required_version.

quiz.q: A production workspace is VCS-driven with auto-apply on. Developers have only Read on the workspace but can merge to the repository's main branch. A reviewer calls this a privilege path. What is it?
choices: Read access includes the right to confirm applies
Policy sets give merge rights to teams automatically
Anyone who can merge to the linked branch can queue plans, and with auto-apply the merge starts the apply
Speculative plans on pull requests can be applied by the author
quiz.explain: HCP Terraform permissions do not cover the connected VCS, and merge rights act as write access. Choice A is wrong because Read does not confirm, choice B invents a behaviour, and choice D is wrong because speculative plans cannot be applied.

quiz.q: A module `s3_logs` is called with `version = "~> 2.1"` from the private registry. A maintainer renames the output `bucket_arn` to `arn` in release 2.4.0 and callers fail at plan. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The release was backward compatible because the lock file holds module versions
The rename is a breaking change for an interface that callers depend on, so it belongs in a major release, ideally after keeping the old output for a while
Callers should switch the call to a Git source with `version = "2.4.0"`
Only ephemeral outputs may be renamed within a minor release
quiz.explain: Outputs are part of the module contract and semantic versioning puts breaking changes in major releases. Choice A is wrong because module versions are not locked, choice C is wrong because version does not apply to Git, and choice D invents a rule.

days.recap: Know 90 minutes, multiple choice, Terraform 1.15 and scenario style. Domains: trace addresses, keep secrets out of state, use dynamic credentials and scoped policy sets, treat modules and versions as contracts, and remember where HCP Terraform runs execute. Eliminate options that are real but misplaced.
